title: Slide 1 · Self-Supervised Learning and Embeddings
question: Can the readings [2, 4, 6] supply an input and a target for training without a person labeling the trend?
answer: Yes. Give the first two readings to the model and save 6 as the target. Keeping 6 hidden matters: if it appears in the input, copying it would solve the task.

title: Slide 2 · Make a target from the record
question: A classmate creates two slightly different copies of each record, then randomly splits all copies. What might go wrong?
answer: Nearly identical versions could occur in training and testing. Split by original record first and keep its derived views together.

title: Slide 3 · Encode the visible part and reconstruct the hidden part
question: Why does the fit give approximately [−1, 1] on these records?
answer: In every example c − b equals b − a. We can compute that change with −1 times the first reading and +1 times the second. The training inputs include independent directions, so these weights are identified here.

title: Slide 4 · Ask what the embedding preserves
question: Can a predictor using only z determine whether the second reading exceeds 8?
answer: No. The first two examples have z = 2, but only [7, 9] passes that threshold. Keeping the second reading would resolve the ambiguity.

title: Slide 5 · Compare two embeddings by their direction
question: Why might cosine be a poor choice if absolute jump size determines the class?
answer: [1, 0] and [10, 0] get cosine 1 with the query. A feature or distance that retains magnitude would make the jump-size difference available.

title: Slide 6 · Make positive and negative pairs
question: Suppose a different rising record is treated as a negative. Why might that matter?
answer: The two records have distinct identities, but share the downstream trend class. Pushing them apart may suppress useful shared structure. Such a negative is called a false negative relative to that downstream meaning.

title: Slide 7 · Write a loss that rewards the right match
question: If a third alternative has score 0, what happens to the first example’s loss?
answer: The numerator remains e. The denominator increases from e + 1 to e + 2. The positive probability falls from about 0.731 to 0.576, so the loss rises to about 0.551.

title: Slide 8 · See a contrastive objective change a weight
question: Does lowering this loss on one pair show that the encoder can identify every kind of trend?
answer: It shows that the update improves these supplied matches. Test the representation on independent records, including cases unlike this simple pair.

title: Slide 9 · Freeze the encoder and test it on a new task
question: What do four correct predictions by both the trained probe and the raw-change rule tell us? Which benefit of pretraining would need another experiment?
answer: The frozen embedding retains enough information for the probe to recognize these trends. The raw-change rule also gets four of four, so this comparison demonstrates no accuracy gain over that rule. Try noisier records from unseen instruments and evaluate the same frozen predictors, including the baseline, on the same examples.

title: Slide 11 · From this module to the next
question: If a query gives two earlier readings equal scores and both are allowed, how much weight will each get after exponential normalization?
answer: Equal scores give equal positive weights. With only those two candidates, dividing by their sum gives one half to each. The next module uses those weights to combine the values at the two positions.

title: Office hours · How can a method be supervised by something other than a person?
question: How can a method be supervised by something other than a person?
answer: A recorded value or a known relationship supplies the answer to a deliberately constructed task. We can hide one measured value or record that two crops came from the same source. A person still chooses what counts as a meaningful task or transformation.

title: Office hours · Is a low reconstruction error enough to choose an embedding?
question: Is a low reconstruction error enough to choose an embedding?
answer: Consider a decoder with access to the whole unmasked input. It could copy the answer and ignore the embedding. Inspect what information enters each path, then test whether the embedding helps on a separate task.

title: Office hours · Why freeze the encoder while evaluating the probe?
question: Why freeze the encoder while evaluating the probe?
answer: It lets you test what a simple classifier can already read from the representation. Updating the encoder and classifier together is fine-tuning and measures what the system can learn after receiving downstream labels.

title: Office hours · Should an embedding always stay the same when I add noise or change brightness?
question: Should an embedding always stay the same when I add noise or change brightness?
answer: That depends on the desired task and the size of the change. A constant offset preserves the signed change of our synthetic trace. It changes the answer to questions about absolute brightness. Test the proposed transformation against the downstream question.

title: Exercise 1
question: Design a masked prediction task for [4, 7, 10]. Name the visible input, hidden target and one way to leak the answer.
answer: For last-reading prediction, show [4, 7] and hide 10. Passing the full record, or giving the mean of all three readings alongside the first two, would reveal the target.

title: Exercise 2
question: Use z = b − a to encode [5, 7] and [1, 3]. Which downstream question could distinguish these inputs: trend direction or second reading above 5?
answer: Both embeddings are 2, and both records rise. The second readings lie on opposite sides of 5. The embedding cannot distinguish that fact. Retaining b alongside z would allow both tasks.

title: Exercise 3
question: Rank [0, 2], [4, 3] and [5, 0] by cosine with [1, 0]. Give the three cosines.
answer: [5,0] scores 1, [4,3] scores 4/5 = 0.8, and [0,2] scores 0. Cosine measures angle here.

title: Exercise 4
question: One anchor has three candidates. The positive has score 0, while the others have scores 0 and ln(2). At temperature 1, find the positive probability and loss.
answer: The total is 4. The positive receives 1/4, so the loss is −ln(1/4) = ln(4), about 1.386. The most similar alternative gets half of the probability.

title: Exercise 5
question: The model should retrieve the same written digit across photographs. Two distinct photographs of the same digit are used as negatives. What assumption caused the problem, and how might you investigate it?
answer: A different source image was assumed to mean a different semantic object or class. Inspect difficult negative pairs with available digit labels, then compare retrieval on an independent labeled set under alternative pair-selection rules.

title: Exercise 6
question: Probe-training class means are −1 and +3. Use the midpoint rule on test embeddings 0, 1.5 and 4 with labels falling, rising and falling. Report accuracy and name the error.
answer: The threshold is 1. Predictions are falling, rising, rising. Two of three are correct. The final example is a false rising prediction. Its original record would help diagnose why its embedding falls on that side.

title: Module overview · Self-Supervised Learning and Embeddings
question: What is this module about?
answer:
Self-Supervised Learning and Embeddings. By the end of this module, you should be able to:
• Describe a self-supervised objective and the information it uses.
• Implement a simple contrastive or reconstruction-based task.
• Evaluate embeddings with similarity and downstream probes.
